result: TGAC8 mice exhibit sustained cardiac hyperdynamic function characterized by ~30% increases in heart rate, ejection fraction, and cardiac output, with only mild blood pressure elevation, and adapt to this increased workload for up to a year without signs of heart failure or excessive mortality.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C19-C22 are supported by echocardiographic data (Figure 1A-E) and citations to prior work. The measurements show consistent increases in HR, EF, and CO, with stroke volume unchanged and blood pressure only mildly elevated. The claim of adaptation for up to a year is supported by prior published studies (Lipskaia et al., 2000; Georget et al., 2002; Georget et al., 2003; Mougenot et al., 2019).

result: TGAC8 hearts show thicker LV walls with reduced cavity volume but no increase in total LV mass, absence of classical pathological hypertrophy markers (MYH7, ANP, BNP), though α-skeletal actin is increased.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C23-C32 are well-supported by echocardiographic measurements (Figure 1F-L) and Western blot data (Figure 2A). The data consistently show increased wall thickness, reduced cavity volume, no change in total LV mass, and absence of pathological hypertrophy markers. The increase in α-skeletal actin is noted but does not contradict the overall conclusion of absence of pathological hypertrophy.

result: TGAC8 hearts harbor an increased number of smaller cardiac myocytes with altered size distribution, without increased collagen content.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C33-C35 are supported by histological analysis (Figure 2B-D) and collagen staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The data show smaller average myocyte size, different size distribution, and no increase in collagen content. This structural remodeling is consistent with the observed thicker walls without increased total mass.

result: TGAC8 hearts show 3-fold higher EdU labeling primarily in non-cardiac myocytes (vimentin-positive interstitial cells and endothelial cells), with no increase in cardiomyocyte S-phase activity.
evaluation: Claims C7, C36-C38 are supported by EdU labeling (Figure 3A-H) and BrdU labeling in MHC-nLAC transgenic mice (Figure 3I-K). The data clearly show increased proliferation in non-cardiac myocytes but not in cardiomyocytes. This suggests increased proliferation of supporting cell types rather than cardiomyocyte proliferation.

result: TGAC8 hearts show markedly increased AC8 expression (8-9-fold) and AC activity (50% increase), with increased PKA catalytic subunit (65.6%), decreased PKA regulatory subunit (26.7%), and increased PKA activity (57.8%).
evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by immunolabeling (Figure 4A-B), AC activity assay (Figure 4C), Western blot (Figure 4D-E), and PKA activity assay (Figure 4F). The data consistently demonstrate enhanced AC/PKA signaling, which is expected given the transgenic overexpression of AC8.

result: TGAC8 hearts show upregulation of key proteins involved in cardiac contractility: αMHC (18.7%), SERCA2 (62.0%), L-type Ca Channel (61.8%), NCX1 (117.6%), CaMKII (35.0%), and RyR2 (66%).
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 4G-K) and immunolabeling (Figure 4L). The upregulation of these proteins is consistent with the observed increased cardiac contractility and provides a molecular basis for the enhanced cardiac performance.

result: TGAC8 hearts show 40% higher protein synthesis rate with increased expression of proteins involved in PKA-mediated protein synthesis pathways (p21Ras, p-c-Raf, MEK1/2, CREB1, CITED4, MSK1, MNK1).
evaluation: Claims C8, C50-C55 are supported by SUnSET assay (Figure 5A) and Western blot data (Figure 5B-G). The increased protein synthesis and upregulation of synthesis-related proteins are consistent with the need to maintain cellular function under chronic stress.

result: TGAC8 hearts show increased proteasome activity with increased soluble misfolded proteins but no accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates, suggesting enhanced protein quality control with increased HSP90α (24%).
evaluation: Claims C9, C56-C59 are supported by proteasome activity assay (Figure 6A) and protein aggregation assays (Figure 6B-C). The data suggest that despite increased protein synthesis and stress, protein quality control mechanisms prevent accumulation of toxic protein aggregates.

result: TGAC8 hearts show enhanced autophagy with increased expression of autophagy proteins (ATG13, PARKIN, ATG4B, PI3Kc3) and increased autophagolysosomes in LV myocytes.
evaluation: Claims C10, C60-C64 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 6E-H) and confocal microscopy (Figure 6I-J). The multiple lines of evidence consistently demonstrate enhanced autophagy, which is an important adaptive mechanism for maintaining cellular homeostasis under chronic stress.

result: TGAC8 hearts show mild increases in damaged mitochondria (0.3% number, 0.4% volume) but no change in healthy mitochondria, with preserved mPTP-ROS threshold indicating maintained mitochondrial fitness.
evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by transmission electron microscopy and stereological analysis (Figure 7G-J) and mPTP-ROS threshold measurements (Figure 7M-N). The data suggest that despite chronic stress, mitochondrial quality control mechanisms maintain overall mitochondrial fitness.

result: TGAC8 hearts show no increase in superoxide radical accumulation despite increased cardiac workload, with increased NRF2 protein (24%) suggesting enhanced ROS defense mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C11, C70-C71 are supported by EPR spectroscopy (Figure 8A) and Western blot (Figure 8B). The maintained ROS levels despite increased energy demands suggest effective antioxidant defense mechanisms, with NRF2 playing a key role.

result: In vivo LV ATP and phosphocreatine levels in TGAC8 do not differ from WT despite increased energy demands.
evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by in vivo MR spectroscopy data (Figure 9C-E). This finding is remarkable given the increased cardiac workload and suggests that energy production mechanisms are adequately upregulated to meet the increased demands.

result: Unbiased omics analyses identified 2,323 differentially expressed transcripts (1,201 up, 1,117 down) and 2,184 differentially expressed proteins (2,026 up, 158 down) in TGAC8 vs WT.
evaluation: Claims C15, C72-C75, C77-C80 are supported by RNASEQ and proteomic data (Figure 10A). The large number of differentially expressed genes and proteins indicates widespread transcriptional and translational changes in response to chronic AC8 overexpression.

result: Human ADCY8 transcript abundance in TGAC8 is >100-fold higher than endogenous mouse isoform; Sprr1a is the most abundantly overexpressed transcript and protein; GO terms cover nearly all biological processes and compartments.
evaluation: Claims C76, C81-C82 are supported by RNASEQ data (Figure 10—figure supplement 1E), omics analysis (Supplementary file 1i), and WebGestalt analysis (Figure 10B). These findings confirm the transgene expression and demonstrate the widespread nature of the adaptive response.

result: IPA analysis identified 248 differentially enriched canonical pathways in transcriptome and 308 in proteome (p<0.05), with 154 activated pathways showing moderate correlation (rs=0.57); 'leukocyte extravasation signaling' was the top differentially regulated pathway.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by IPA analysis results (Supplementary files 1f-g, Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 2). The pathway analysis provides insight into the biological processes altered in TGAC8, with the surprising finding of leukocyte extravasation signaling being most prominent.

result: 544 transcripts and proteins both differed by genotype, with 80.5% showing concordant changes (same direction).
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by omics data analysis (Figure 10A, Figure 10—figure supplement 4). The high concordance between transcript and protein changes suggests that many of the transcriptional changes result in corresponding protein-level changes.

result: Top activated pathways in TGAC8 include Nrf2 signaling, Integrin Signaling, and Cardiac Hypertrophy Signaling, while fatty acid β-oxidation, tryptophan degradation III, isoleucine degradation, and glutaryl Co-A degradation were markedly suppressed.
evaluation: Claims C89-C95 are supported by IPA analysis (Figure 10C). These pathway changes suggest a coordinated metabolic shift and activation of protective signaling pathways in response to chronic stress.

result: TGAC8 hearts show a metabolic shift from fatty acid oxidation to aerobic glycolysis with increased utilization of the pentose phosphate shunt and nucleotide synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are supported by bioinformatic analyses showing reduced expression of fatty acid oxidation enzymes and increased expression of glycolytic and pentose phosphate pathway enzymes (Figure 12), and IPA pathway analysis (Figure 10C). However, these are inferences from gene/protein expression data without direct metabolic flux measurements, which would strengthen the conclusion.

result: ACC2 protein levels were increased in TGAC8 vs WT.
evaluation: Claim C13 is supported by immunolabeling data (Figure 12—figure supplement 3A). The increase in ACC2 is consistent with the proposed metabolic shift and may contribute to reduced fatty acid oxidation and increased glucose utilization.

result: Hsp90α protein levels were increased by 24% in TGAC8 vs WT.
evaluation: Claim C12 is supported by Western blot data (Figure 6D). This increase is consistent with enhanced protein quality control mechanisms in TGAC8.

result: TGAC8 mice have a reduced (~30%) median life span, and later in life (~12 months) develop marked LV fibrosis and dilated cardiomyopathy.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by citation to prior work (Mougenot et al., 2019) and stated in the text. This finding indicates that while the adaptive mechanisms are effective in young adult mice, they eventually fail, leading to heart failure. This is an important limitation of the model and suggests that chronic stress eventually overwhelms protective mechanisms.
